text: He had been working on the memoir for six years when a cousin wrote to him.
His father had left in April, and the family had moved out before the winter he describes.
I was reading the memoir on a plane when I realized I had met one of the people in it.
By the time I reached chapter nine, the narrator had already lied to me twice.
By the time I got there, they had already made the decision.
We had been working on it for two years before anything moved.
I was reading the file when the call came through.
In hindsight, the warning had been there from the first meeting.
That part I remember clearly. The rest I have probably rebuilt.

I have never once told a story in the order it happened, and I have stopped apologising for it. The reason is not literary, it is practical. If I begin at the beginning, the reader has to carry forty pages of backstory before anything is at stake, and nobody carries it. They put the book down at page nine and they are very polite about it later. So I start in the middle of a bad afternoon, and then, once the reader already wants to know why this woman is sitting in a car outside her own house, I go back. That is the moment the past perfect earns its keep. She had left that morning. She had been planning it for a year. And the year arrives as an explanation rather than as homework. My editor tells me I overuse the device, and she is right, and I am going to keep doing it, because the alternative is a book that nobody finishes.

When I take a statement about something that happened three years ago, I do not start with the event. I start with the day around it. What you were doing that morning, what the weather was like, who else was in the building, whether you had eaten. It sounds like small talk and it is not. Two things happen. The first is that the ordinary detail brings the rest back, because memory is stored next to the boring parts, not next to the dramatic ones. The second is that it shows me quite quickly which sections are remembered and which are reconstructed, and that distinction is worth more to me than confidence is. A witness who says he cannot remember whether the door was open is a better witness than one who is certain about everything, and any judge who has been doing the job for a while knows it too.
When the photograph arrived, he had already written the chapter.
I was reading the last chapter when the plane landed.
She had been writing the book for eleven years before anybody saw a page.
By the time the statement was taken, three years had passed.
In hindsight, the twist had been in front of me since chapter one.
He glosses over the year that mattered most.
By the time I got there, they had already made the decision.
We had been working on it for two years before anything moved.
I was reading the file when the call came through.
In hindsight, the warning had been there from the first meeting.
That part I remember clearly. The rest I have probably rebuilt.
